pages.name: Fifty readings
pages.text: Each reading starts at the true value, 27.00 V, drawn dashed. Twelve pegs nudge it left or right on the way down. The nudges scatter the readings with a standard deviation of 0.04 V. That is the random error. Fifty readings pile up round 27.00 V. Most land within about 0.08 V either side. So a single reading could be any one of these beads.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings fall from a hopper over the true value, 27.00 volts, through a field of pegs, and pile up on a beam balanced at their mean. A bracket under the beam marks where most of them land.

pages.name: One reading
pages.task: One reading off this meter says 27.06 V. It is ringed. What can you say about the true voltage?
pages.answer: It is probably within about 0.08 V of 27.06 V
pages.why: One reading carries its own random error. Most readings land within about 0.08 V of the true value. So the true value is probably within about 0.08 V of the reading. Here it is 27.00 V, inside that reach.

pages.name: Average a few
pages.text: Here each bead is the mean of four readings. The random errors of the readings in a bead point different ways, so they partly cancel. With two a bead the pile narrows to about seven tenths of its width. With four it is half as wide. It still centres on 27.00 V. So the spread of a mean is the spread of one reading divided by the square root of how many are averaged.
pages.alt: The pile of fifty simulated beads under the peg field. Each bead can be the mean of one, two or four readings; the more it averages, the closer the pegs and the narrower the pile.

pages.name: Mean of four
pages.task: One reading's random error is 0.04 V. Each bead is the mean of four readings. What is the beads' standard deviation?
pages.why: Four readings a bead divide the spread by √4, which is 2. So 0.04 V ÷ 2 = 0.02 V. The bracket shows 1 SD each side of the mean.

pages.name: The result
pages.text: Back to one reading a bead. The bracket over the pile is the result. It is the mean of all fifty, ± its [[uncertainty]]. By the square-root rule, that mean spreads 0.04 ÷ √50. Twice a spread either side catches about 95%, as the 0.08 V does for single readings. So the result reaches 2 × 0.04 ÷ √50 either side. With √50 about 7.07, that is about 0.011 V. Give the value to the same decimal place: 27.000 ± 0.011 V. The wide bracket under the beam shows where most single readings land.
pages.alt: The pile of fifty single readings with a narrow bracket over it, the result, and a wide bracket under the beam where most beads fall.

pages.name: The next reading
pages.task: The fifty readings give a result of 27.000 ± 0.011 V. The next single reading says 27.05 V. Is something wrong?
pages.answer: No. Single readings scatter much wider than the result
pages.why: The result says where the mean of fifty sits. Single readings scatter much wider, within about 0.08 V either side. 27.05 V is 0.05 V out, inside that. So nothing is wrong.

pages.name: A coarser meter
pages.text: Here the meter reads to 0.05 V, so the beads sit in bricks one step wide. That step is the meter's [[resolution]]. Rounding can put a reading up to half a step, 0.025 V, from what the meter sensed. The mean of many still lands close to 27.00 V. A fine step is not the same as an accurate meter.
pages.alt: The pile of fifty simulated readings in columns one step of the meter wide, with one step named over the tallest column. On a meter that reads to 0.05 volts the readings stack into wide bricks.

pages.name: Read the rating
pages.task: A meter rated ±(1% + 3 digits) shows 50.0 V. It reads to 0.1 V. Where could the true voltage be?
pages.why: 1% of 50.0 V is 0.5 V. Three digits are three steps of 0.1 V, so 0.3 V. Together that is 0.8 V either side. So the true voltage could be anywhere from 49.2 V to 50.8 V.

pages.name: Reads high
pages.text: Here the meter reads 0.02 V high, and each bead is the mean of four readings. The shaded window is an example meter's accuracy, 0.047 V either side of 27.00 V. A meter within its rating can centre anywhere inside it. The whole pile has shifted across. Averaging tightened it round 27.02 V, where the meter centres. The result, 27.020 ± 0.006 V, misses the dashed true value. Each fresh batch misses it too. The offset lands on every reading, so it lands on their mean too. That is a [[systematic error]].
pages.alt: The peg field and pile under a shaded window round the true value as wide as the meter's accuracy. The hopper sits where the meter centres, a narrow bracket over the pile marks the result and a wide one under the beam marks where most beads fall.

pages.name: Reading 0.03 V high
pages.task: This meter reads 0.03 V high. You make each bead the mean of four readings instead of one. Where does the result centre now?
pages.answer: Near 27.03 V, with a narrower bracket
pages.why: Averaging four readings halves the random scatter, so the bracket narrows. But the 0.03 V offset is in every reading, so it is in their mean too. The result still centres near 27.03 V.
pages.alt: The peg field and pile with the hopper 0.03 volts above the true value, inside the accuracy window, and the whole pile shifted that way.
options: Near 27.03 V, with a narrower bracket
Near 27.00 V, as averaging cancels the error
Near 27.015 V, halfway

pages.name: Against a limit
pages.text: With four readings a bead, a dashed example upper limit sits at 27.02 V. Here the meter reads 0.02 V high, and the result overlaps the limit. From the readings alone, the true value could be either side. So it shows neither a pass nor a fail. At 0 and 0.01 V high the result sits below the limit. At 0.03 V it sits above, so the readings say fail. Yet the true value is still 27.00 V. A real bracket must also take in the meter's accuracy.

pages.name: Against a maximum
pages.task: A result is 0.82 ± 0.03 Ω at 95%. The example maximum is 0.84 Ω. What does it show?
pages.answer: Neither a pass nor a fail
pages.why: The bracket runs from 0.82 − 0.03 = 0.79 Ω to 0.82 + 0.03 = 0.85 Ω. It overlaps the 0.84 Ω maximum. So the true value could be either side, and the result shows neither a pass nor a fail. A real bracket must also take in the meter's accuracy.

pages.name: A finer display
pages.task: Your meter reads to 0.05 V and reads 0.02 V high. You switch to one that reads to 0.01 V, with the same 0.02 V offset. What gets better?
pages.answer: Each reading shows a finer step, but the offset stays
pages.why: Resolution and offset are separate. The finer display shows each reading to 0.01 V, so the bricks become narrow columns. But every reading is still 0.02 V high, so the pile still centres near 27.02 V.
